title: Cloudera Pays $2 Million, Accepts Two-Year PERM Ban in US Worker Discrimination Settlement
excerpt: The Justice and Labor departments say Cloudera directed PERM applicants to a non-functional email address, failed to consider qualified US workers for seven jobs, and must now fund $1.4 million in back pay, pay $600,000 in penalties and stay out of PERM for two years.
body:
• Cloudera will pay $600,000 in civil penalties and fund up to $1.4 million in back pay for qualified US workers who were not given fair consideration for seven PERM jobs, under a coordinated Justice and Labor department settlement.
  • The company is barred from the PERM program for two years — a debarment the Labor Department had already previewed by suspending Cloudera's PERM processing — and faces enhanced monitoring, revised recruitment procedures and reporting requirements.
  • DOJ alleged that from March 31, 2024 to January 28, 2025 Cloudera used a non-functional email address that made it impossible for some US workers to apply for jobs advertised in connection with PERM certifications.
  • For Indian professionals at Cloudera: the two-year PERM debarment means the company cannot file new permanent labor certifications during that period, so affected employees should ask the company in writing how their green-card timelines will be handled.

Cloudera Inc., the Santa Clara data management company, has agreed to pay $2 million and accept a two-year ban from the PERM program to resolve federal allegations that it discriminated against qualified US workers during green-card recruitment. The settlement, announced by the US Departments of Justice and Labor, is the specific enforcement outcome in Cloudera's case — separate from the broader PERM processing freezes that have hit other technology firms in recent days.

"There are no exceptions: the Justice Department will hold accountable employers who discriminate against U.S. workers."

— Harmeet K. Dhillon, Assistant Attorney General, Civil Rights Division

What the Government Alleged

The Justice Department's Immigrant and Employee Rights Section sued in April, alleging Cloudera violated the Immigration and Nationality Act when recruiting and hiring for seven positions under the PERM process. According to the settlement summary on the Justice Department's settlements page, the company created a non-functional email address that made it impossible for some US workers to apply for jobs it advertised in connection with permanent labor certifications, deterred them from applying, and thus failed to consider them.

https://x.com/livemint/status/2112449169181065473

Cloudera disputes intent. A spokesperson told Bloomberg Law the company took immediate corrective action when it learned an email address used in its recruitment process was inadvertently limited to internal employees. "Cloudera does not discriminate against anyone in making hiring decisions, and we remain firmly committed to fair, lawful, and open recruitment practices," the spokesperson said.

The Settlement Terms, in Full

The money breaks into two parts: $600,000 in civil penalties to the United States, and a back-pay fund of up to $1.4 million to compensate qualified US workers who tried to apply for the jobs at issue but were not given fair consideration. Beyond the money, Cloudera must conduct recruitment for PERM-related positions the same way it conducts recruitment for similar non-PERM positions — hiring recruiters, posting on its career website and entering candidates in its central applicant-tracking system. It will submit to the Justice Department's training and monitoring requirements for three years.

The Labor Department side of the deal is the sanction with the longest tail. The two-year debarment follows DOL's earlier suspension of Cloudera's PERM processing, which Bloomberg Law described as an unprecedented enforcement action at the time. The agreement also resolves that suspension, counts a two-year self-debarment period running since Cloudera's last PERM withdrawal, and includes a commitment to join the Department of War's SkillBridge program.

Why This Matters Beyond Cloudera

PERM is the first step in most employment-based green cards: an employer may sponsor a foreign worker for permanent residence only after demonstrating that qualified US workers were given a genuine opportunity to apply and that no qualified, willing and available US worker could be found. The Justice Department said this is the fourteenth settlement since it relaunched its Protecting US Workers Initiative in 2025, following earlier high-dollar agreements involving firms including Meta, Apple and OpenAI. Officials said the Cloudera framework — penalties, back pay and debarment together — will serve as a precedent for future enforcement.

For Indian H-1B holders, the direct impact is narrow but real: it is Cloudera's own PERM pipeline that is frozen for two years, not the wider tech sector's. Employees sponsored by other employers are not affected by this settlement, though the separate PERM freezes reported at Microsoft, Adobe and other firms remain unresolved and unspecified. Workers who believe they were blocked from applying for one of the seven Cloudera jobs can contact the Immigrant and Employee Rights Section's free worker hotline at 1-800-255-7688; employers can call 1-800-255-8155.

What Happens Next

Cloudera now operates under monitoring while its PERM debarment runs. For other employers, the lesson is concrete: a broken application channel in PERM recruitment is no longer treated as an administrative error.
